utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Wednesday, June 24th, 2009, and I greet Mr. Praljak as well as Mr. Pusic, Petkovic, and Stojic. I also greet those who unfortunately are not here with us for various reasons. I welcome Defence counsels, Mr. Stringer, and his associates, and everyone else helping us in the courtroom. The Trial Chamber will issue an oral decision regarding the dead-lines for the submission -- the filing of IC lists. This is the title of the oral decision: Oral decision for modification of dead-lines regarding filing of IC lists after the testimony of accused Praljak. Through an oral decision of June 22nd, 2009, the parties were informed of the dead-lines they were to abide with after the testimony of accused Praljak regarding the filing of their IC lists to admit documents, to make objections to these IC lists, and to eventually reply to the objections, to possibly reply to the objections.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber recalls that these are dead-lines provided for in the guide-line number 8, provided for in the decision on the adoption of guide-lines regarding the presentation of Defence evidence. During the hearing of June 22nd, 2009, the Praljak Defence and the Prosecution sought leave from the Trial Chamber in order to obtain extension of the dead-lines provided for in the oral decision. Given the volume expected -- the volume of documents expected, which may be -- for which admission may be sought by the parties, the Trial Chamber decides to exceptionally grant leave to the Praljak and to the Prosecution motions. Therefore, the Trial Chamber decides to modify its oral decision of June 22nd, 2009, only as far as dead-lines are concerned. And the Trial Chamber also requests all parties to abide by the following dead-lines. IC lists regarding the request to admit exhibits must be filed three days after the last day of Mr. -- the accused Praljak's testimony. The filing of the objections regarding these IC lists must occur within seven days after the filing of the IC lists. The filing of any possible replies to these objections must be made three days after the filing of the -- of the objections. This is the decision. So once Mr. Praljak is finished with his testimony, within the three days after that date the IC lists will have to be filed. Should there be any objections, they will have to be filed within seven days and should there be any replies to the objections this filing should be done within three next days. It's a bit complicated, but I'm sure that when you read the document -- when you read the decision it will be very clear. I hope that thanks to this decision everyone will work properly. It is true that there are a lot of documents and that an extension was absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. I will now finish with my questions. I hope I'll be finished today. Normally I should. I have about 12 documents to show you, documents that I want to put questions to you about. After that, as I told you earlier, I will be asking you questions about sniping regarding seven casualties, but we'll come to that later. Let's take a look at document -- at the document on the screen. It's document P 00742. As you see, Mr. Praljak, this is a document issued by the minister of Croatia -- by the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Ministry of Defence, dated November 14, 1992, this is an order following a request that allegedly you would have made and asking for the transfer of a number of officers from the Split Operative Zone to Capljina. Your counsels mentioned this document. Could you tell us what the purpose of showing this document -- what is the purpose of showing this document, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers in question were in Split. I spoke to them. And they agreed to go for a month to Central Bosnia, to Travnik, Novi Travnik, and other places. After the fall of Jajce and after we witnessed the lack of organisation among the HVO units and among the BiH units, I went to the Split Operations Zone and I spoke to people and asked around to see who would be willing to spend a month in that area and to help organise the military there. This means that I asked for a gunman, a signalsman who would be establishing communication, a person in charge of the organisation of the brigade there, one person who would explain how to set up the line, and so on and so forth. A few people volunteered but not everybody left. At first there were eight and finally we agreed that five would suffice and five people indeed went to Central Bosnia to assist both the HVO and the BiH army, to organise themselves as I've just explained. They stayed there only a month and then they returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now move to paragraph 192 which deals with what happened in Stupni Do, and we will take a look at a document that we have already seen but I believe that it is important to take a look at it again, P 06026. On the screen we have the English version but most importantly we have the B/C/S original, a document that I went -- that I fetched this morning very early in order to really scrutinise it, at the crack of dawn. General Praljak, this is a document, it's a report by Mr. Rajic and sent to Mr. Kordic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Blaskic, as well as Mr. Mario Bradara. This document dates back to October 23rd, 1993. There is an incoming mail stamp October 28, 1993 -- 93, actually. This document was officially registered under the number 5021. In this document Mr. Rajic is reporting on the attacks by the MOS in the Bobovac responsibility area. He is mentioning also what is happening in Stupni Do, saying that the Muslims have set up their forces and that -- he says that there was an attack in the morning Bogos. He explains that a number of members of the MOS were killed along with some civilians. Regarding HVO casualties he says that there were two persons killed and seven wounded. He continues saying that Pejcinovic Duznovic and Gavran had been placed in isolation. Also on the document we have some things that are handwritten, the word Petkovic that was underlined as well as the three names that I mentioned that were also underlined, Pejcinovic, Duznovic and Gavran, and two sentences have been added also. My first question is this one, Mr. Praljak: Is this your handwriting, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Second question: When did you learn of this document? I see that there's this stamp for incoming mail dated October 28th. Does this mean that you obtained this document at that date or did you know about it before that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the 23rd of October, 1993, around 11.00 in the evening, 2300 hours approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I unearthed a translation problem regarding the handwritten sentence. In the Rajic judgement, the beginning of the sentence is translated as follows: "Sort out," whereas in the document we have here it says "deal." I don't understand why we have this "sort out" in the Rajic judgement without any footnote that could help anyone understand what document is referred to in these conclusions. So to make things clear, Mr. Praljak, could you please very slowly read out the handwritten sentence, the first handwritten sentence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sort out the situation in Vares without any mercy shown towards anybody. "Find people who are up to the time and task" -- could you scroll up a little bit, please. Thank you. "... those who are up to the time and task."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Reading the sentence -- getting the French translation from this sentence is "settle the situation in Vares" or "sort out the situation in Vares" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, which is the same thing as "deal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... judgement is sort out. Mr. Registrar, could we have the last page of the English document, please. As you see, on the second page we don't have "sort out" but "deal with," sort out or deal. I don't understand why it's not the exact same words that are used.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... deal are synonyms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is important, Mr. Praljak, because in the Rajic judgement it says that you were ordered to settle the situation in Vares without mercy towards anyone, but there's absolutely no reference to the content of the document. Any reasonable trier of fact looking at this could conclude that through this order he asked for everyone to be killed. So we need to look at the document. First question, Mr. Praljak: When Mr. Rajic wrote this report, there's always been -- there's already been casualties. He says in his report that there were casualties on both sides. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Mr. Rajic made his report after the events?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So saying "show no mercy" cannot be applied retroactively. There already are casualties anyway.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but this does not refer -- it does not at all refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wondered, and I wish -- I hope that you can shed some light on this, I really wondered why it said "deal with the situation." Maybe I'm making a mistake, but you underlined these three names and you also added something in handwriting. So isn't there -- I was wondering whether there was a link between these names that were underlined and what you wrote, settling the situation of the three that are in isolation, and if there errors were made or mistakes were made, show no mercy, even though these are people from the HVO, which might explain why you said it to be so tough and to show no mercy towards anyone. Is this the real interpretation or should there be another one?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a good interpretation. He isolated men. The situation was unclear even before and this is how it's said in Croatian, this is how I normally say it. Petkovic, deal with that situation, sort it out, Petkovic, because there's a state of disorder. With whoever, whatever is happening (sentence unclear). And the second sentence is: Find men who are up to the situation. I believe that anybody faced with such a situation would say that, and I believe that the same phrase is used in other languages as well. Deal with the situation. There is a state of disorder. Some people have been isolated. I am not privy to all the facts, but I understand the situation, I adhere by what I said, this was sent to Petkovic and Petkovic fully understands what I'm writing to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to place a paragraph 39 of the judgement under the ELMO. Mr. Usher, could we please have that. Can you please put this paragraph of the judgement under the ELMO. It's in English but all counsels will be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, may I address the Trial Chamber very briefly. Perhaps now is a good time. During the last series of questions about the sort out versus "deal with" language that's in the English translation, the interpreters on the English channel a couple times made clarifications or comments which only appear in the record partially. I'm looking at line 15 of page 6 and then also page 17, and because the President has noticed that there is a difference between the translations "deal with" and "sort out," could I suggest that the interpreter's full clarification be put on the record because it doesn't appear there at the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll try to solve this. If there's a problem we'll ask the CLSS to make -- to do the translation. Mr. Praljak, could you please read again this first handwritten sentence slowly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sort out or deal with the situation in Vares showing no mercy towards anybody." Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a problem with translation. The English interpreters said "sort out or deal" -- for them it's the same thing, it means the same thing.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. The root of the word "srediti" in Croatian is the word "order," "Ordnung." "Ordnung," which is read "order" -- it's not "order." No, no, it's not. I'm not going to go into English because I don't speak English. "Ordnung" in German. There is something that is not order, non-"Ordnung," chaos. And the word "sort out" or "deal with" or "srediti" in Croatian means to re-instate order in the courtroom, in the street, in a company in the police, deal with the situation, install order, and this is the correct explanation of the Croatian word "srediti" which means "install order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now I wanted to have paragraph 39 on the ELMO. When you read it as it is in the judgement, it looks like you ordered Mr. Rajic to show no mercy and that this order was known by local HVO commanders and so that because of this there might be a very aggressive attitude against the Bosnian Muslims in the Vares area. Now what paragraph 39 forgets to mention is that this handwritten sentence was added after the events and does not take into account these three Croats who were placed in isolation by Rajic. Let's finish with this document, Mr. Praljak. You said that when you meant sort out the situation it meant --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... so everything comes back to order --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say, by finding men, and how is he going to find men among the Muslims? He has to find men among the Croats and such men that will be up to the situation, faced with the situation, and deal with the situation, install order, sort out the situation. Everything is known here. They received this on the 24th in the morning and they did whatever they had to do. Everything is so clear and has been for such a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a look at the next document, P 06020.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I must confess, Mr. Praljak, that everything is not so clear to me. Restore order, all right. What was the disorder? What did this actually mean? What was the problem that should be solved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, to be quite frank, we cannot start this trial a hundred times all over again. You have documents that came from Emil Harah, from Vares, and from others in that area, a huge pile of documents, and they clearly show the kind of disorder or lack of order that existed there. The brigade commander could no longer do his job, he's asking to be removed from office, he says that he has gone crazy, he receives information about smuggling and all that -- well, it's all in evidence, it's been in evidence for two years in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a follow-up to the question by Judge Trechsel. The fact that the Bobovac Brigade commander is not able to carry out his mission, could this be a reason why a new commander must restore order in the brigade, by orders or by an investigation and that order has to be restored? Is that one way of understanding the text?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how you must understand it. In the document it says that an attack was launched by the BH army, and there is no time for investigations. You do that after the fact. At that time you need to make decisions, instantly, clear, precise decisions. And then later on you can investigate who did what. But in a situation where it says that BH army launched an attack and before that in a whole series of documents -- well, we don't want to go through them again. I'm simply writing an instruction to General Petkovic saying, Petkovic, sort out the situation. Get them out of here. The commander must be removed from office from his post within three minutes and later on you do the paperwork, whereby he's formally removed from his post, but you have to make prompt, instant decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally we'll have a last document, P 06020. This is a report from Emil Harah on -- at 1145 on the 23rd of October. It is sent to you personally. He recounts the events, and towards the end he says that Ivica Rajic insisted that Harah should send you the report. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivica Rajic was superior to -- for that -- in that part of the theatre and then Tihomir Blaskic was the next higher-up instance. This is a simple military report that just shows that the units of the 3rd Corps are attacking the Bobovac Brigade from the areas of Zenica, Kakanj, towards Vares, and then we can see his conviction that another corps of the BH army would help him fight off the 3rd BH Army Corps. And then he says lines are very extended -- well, nothing on the basis of document, I could not reach any conclusions apart from the fact that they are under attack. And that because of this order Vares would fall. That's why I sent this -- the two sentences to Petkovic, that unless there is an immediate and very harsh response to re-introduce order into the situation -- well, I don't have anything to add to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if you will find it inappropriate for me to intervene regarding this document, but protected witness EA spoke about this document and said that it was a forgery, and also in 92 bis statement of a witness who was -- knew about these events, he said that no document of this sort with this kind of signature was ever written. So perhaps this might be of some assistance so that we don't deal with things that are ultimately irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer, we're going to address this. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... simply to say and -- and I think we should address it. My recollection is that there was a different document that the witness talked about. I could be wrong, but I think we should double-check whether in fact this is authentic or not. I had the recollection that there was a different document that Witness EA was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, are you sure that is the right document mentioned by Witness EA as a forgery?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... in the course of the next break I can provide all the references, the transcript pages, and the 92 bis statement where this is indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, as we have these two documents before us, there is one term that comes up in both and it's the word "mop-up." Rajic writes: "The town of Vares has been mopped-up and all Muslims of military age placed under surveillance ..." And in this document Emil Harah also speaks of a Muslim village nearby the town that they mopped-up. How would you translate "mopped-up" or how would you describe what it means?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, to be quite honest, probably as I sit here today we should use another term in Croatian, but that term was so widely used, it's such a usual term if you look -- if you watch movies or read books or papers. I don't know what the English word is but in Croatian you always say it has been "mopped-up," "ocisceno," in terms of there are no military units there, after combat action they have been defeated. This use of the term "ciscenje," "mop-up operation," it's a military term pure and simple. It means all the armed members of the enemy force have been defeated. In the movies you can see it when the units advance they always say it's been mopped-up, it's all clean now. When they go into a building they say "clear," "cisto." It's the same term as used in Croatian. If you look at movies and you have the FBI enter a house or the SWAT teams in New York, in Croatian the word is "cisto" "ocisceno," and this is the sense in which this term was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will also be frank with you, Mr. Praljak, in the context of these proceedings one wonders whether it does not refer to ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. No. In military sense when you say "ciscenje," "mopping-up," that's what it means, what I've just explained to you. The members of the military units of the enemy side have been "ocisceni," "mopped-up." There are no members left, they are not hiding anywhere. It's been cleaned of them, so to speak, and now unfortunately this word "clean" or "cleanse" now has this other meaning of ethnic cleansing, but that's another thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have answered the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, following what Ms. Alaburic said. If this is a forgery I have a very simple first question for you. As far as you can remember, on the 23rd of October, 1993, after 11.45, so maybe the next day or the day after, the 24 or the 25th, were you made aware of a report by Emil Harah?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot answer this question with any kind of reliability, not even theoretically after all these years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the contents of the document. If this is a forgery, it is a forgery that was very well made because we have a number 01-703-1/93. So those who would have made the forgery can run the risk of checking whether there was in the books a document before and one after, a 702 or 704. There is no signature also so one may think this was a message sent by electronic means or by packet. If this is a forgery, why was it done by the authors thereof? What would you say as to the move they had in mind? If you don't have any idea, I could have one for you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, Your Honours. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any reasonable trier of fact, knowing the facts of the case, could he imagine that in sending this report at 11.45 on the 23rd of October would show that you were aware or in the know of the operation that Harah upon instructions by Rajic is busy with the operation, has something else to do than sending written reports, sends you the report so that you be informed in realtime of anything that may happen and everything that happens. And the fact that we have our name here, could it be a reason to conclude that you were in the know of things before, during, and after the event?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you a very specific answer to that question, apart from saying that I do know one thing for a fact and that's that forged documents, documents that were forged in order to support an argument or the case here at this Tribunal, there were many of those. I know that for a fact and I know that some things that relate to Vares, in the press in particular, were blamed on me in such a way to implicate that I knew about the events in Stupni Do before they occurred. I know, however, what I know and I know for a fact that I came to the Main Staff around 2300 hours and I remember only that document and the previous documents, and I know exactly what I thought when I wrote this to Petkovic and I was quite specific in what I wrote and I stand by it. I claim that they are forged documents, including the document with my signature that I approve the release of the prisoners -- well, of the hundreds of documents on the last day when I was not there at all, they tried to foist this on me, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, just bring your attention to the last sentence here which indicates that on that day, the 23rd of October, at around 1100 hours, Ivica Rajic was in Kiseljak because it says here from Kiseljak he is controlling or running the action. So perhaps this might be a key to explain this whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, Ms. Alaburic is telling us that Mr. Rajic was running the operations from Kiseljak whilst he was present on the ground. So this may be an explanation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on the information I received later, Ivica Rajic was not in Kiseljak at the time. So if this is a forgery, obviously the goal was to say, Well, I was not in Vares or anywhere near Vares, I was in Kiseljak. He was not in Kiseljak at the time, and Emil Harah had to know that Ivica Rajic was not in Kiseljak but that he was already doing things in Vares that were not admissible. He tells me, I've placed Muslims under surveillance. He doesn't say, I detained them, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to be much faster now. Indeed we are going to examine a few documents rather cursorily. Paragraph 203, 3D 00278. That's the number of the document. This document is about you. It's going to be on our screens soon. Here it is. It says what your situation is for the administration, and it is clearly said that you had submitted a request as early as the 1st of June seeking permission to leave the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notices that the translation is different in writing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 280, 1D 02962. You are here demonstrating that there was no criminal enterprise because if there was any, how can you account for the fact that the so-called victims would go for a meeting in Zagreb, where they're going to ask for a law to be endorsed by the Croatian government? This is 1D 02942. We've seen this document already. Do you -- are you aware of this document, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In your submissions, this is what you said. Can you give us an explanation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of possibly hundreds of documents, and my case is quite clear. Croatia was - well, how should I put it? - like an open possibility to do whatever they wanted as far as the BH was concerned, and Muslims in particular, sessions of the government, financial assistance, military assistance -- well, they had dozens, hundreds of organisations in Zagreb and all over Croatia, military, civilian, educational, religious, it was open ground for them. They were fomenting propaganda against Croatia in Croatia itself. At times Croatia looked more like the colony of Alija Izetbegovic, the government in Sarajevo, and the BH army. No questions were asked, no requests were made, they never said please, its state and all its institutions used it as it saw fit. I sometimes objected to that. I said, Well, there should be more order here, because you never knew who represented what ministry, what government. Hundreds of those occasions, Your Honours. So -- and now this state is accused of a joint criminal enterprise -- well, I simply cannot see the logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am nearly done. Let's go to the contents of paragraph 346 that deals with a visit by MPs from the Sabor. We've seen this document already; it is 3D 01391. I'll repeat, 3D 01091.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. You're going to see it soon. This is a report by the Assembly, a report by MPs who went to Bosnia and Herzegovina. In paragraph 340 your counsels say that you lobbied the Sabor for MPs to go and visit the Republic of Bosnia in order to have a fact-finding mission and say what the situation was about. So this is a detailed report of the people they have met and of their conclusions following the visit. I noted that the visit was really dependent on the UNPROFOR because the UNPROFOR had to secure their safety and their transport. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It appears that General Wahlgren, in person, was the person in charge of the logistics of this mission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in your recollection, were these MPs always escorted by UNPROFOR servicemen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they went to the eastern side of Mostar and when they were supposed to go to Konjic, Jablanica, and Central Bosnia as they wanted, they had an escort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When reading this report I see that these MPs, who belonged to various parties even though they're all in the national union government, conclude that there was a conflict between the Croatian side and the Muslim side. They cannot assess who originated, who initiated the conflict. In paragraph 4(a), they conclude that the causes of the conflict would be due to different comprehension of the internal system of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What does this mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I've been saying all this time. That's precisely what it means. They understood that -- well, the BH, if the two sides, the Muslim and Croat side, have different ideas about internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Muslims wanted a unitary state based on the one man/one vote principle; and the Croatian approach was that there should be provinces or cantons or some kind of constituent parts, what I used to call some kind of self government for areas or settlements where Croats are in the majority. But if you allow me, Your Honours, I addressed the Croatian Sabor, the parliament, quite violently. They tried to stop me but they couldn't. You have to understand, as the war goes on the politicians and all "smart people" are trying to get as far as they can from the war. They sit in cafes, they meet in Geneva, London, Paris, staying in nice hotels and they talk about what should be done, and they're really smart, they're all being very, very smart. That's how it's done today, and what they're saying is usually based on wrong information. And I was desperate, I was quite angry. It was my demand, You should go. And then they, Your Honours, they who are still involved in the war, who are still suffering through it, they're to blame, they're the scapegoats. Well, agree, we have a solution, everybody's saying that. And I'm telling them, Well, come down here, and they say, Well, Praljak's stupid, Praljak simply doesn't want the war, please make an arrangement with the other side and put a stop to the war. Praljak and Petkovic and all the others in the HVO don't want to have the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you've said this already. In the conclusions under (c) and (d) of paragraph 4, this is put down to part of the Muslim sides that openly rejected the Vance-Owen Plan and they were, so does the text say, the provocateurs. But I've noted something else, but there's no solution suggested in the conclusions, unfortunately so. They've noted that there were crimes, and it is said that individuals in uniform with pro-fascist insignia committed crimes in Muslim villages. And it is said that they must be identified and punished. So this delegation of MPs has realised that there have been crimes in Muslim villages, and we can better understand this sentence when we know that the MPs met with an SDA delegation. The very fact that these MPs knew and wrote in this report that crimes had been committed, was this something they told you? Did they tell you that these people had to be punished? Were you made aware of this, this thing that they noticed in April?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I knew that even without them. That's why I asked for them to go down there and try and put a stop to the war. We can go on investigating, we have investigated things, people have been punished for the crimes they committed, they will continue being punished, but the war would go on resulting in casualties. And their duty is to stop the war and to say precisely who is the one who's behind the war, who's causing the war to go on. I was in Croatia and I was not in a place to be in charge of the investigation of any crimes. I was just here as a person who completely understood the situation, fully, completely, why things happened, what's going to go on happening, and with what result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still want to take a look at paragraph 366 on cooperation between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. The document is 3D 00299. This is a letter by Hasan Efendic to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia on January 4th, 1993. The document is on the screen. In your submissions you mention this document. What is the importance of this document to your defence case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To confirm what I've been saying all this time, which is that vis-a-vis the volunteers from the Croatian army, Muslims, Croatia treated them in the same way as they treated Croats. Here you see a request is being made for a colonel, a major, and a doctor, also a colonel, to be allowed to join the BH army and still keep the status in the Croatian army as is -- as was laid out from the very outset. You have been fighting in the Croatian army and now your first or second homeland has come under attack. You can go and fight for your second or first homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we will not rob you of your bare essentials, which is social security, a pension fund, and salaries in the Croatian army. Once you finish your mission there, once you were defeated or come victorious, we will take you back because that's the only honest and logical thing to do because it was our joint fight. The same thing applied to Muslims as it did Croats, and I claim that a lot more Muslims from Croatia or via Croatia, trained in Croatia, went to fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina than Croats. But this does not take into account the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last document, P 00149. It deals with the diplomatic relations between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. In your submissions you say that these relations were excellent. This is a letter sent by Mr. Tudjman to Mr. Izetbegovic, as you see, dated April 7th, 1992, and recognising the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state. I'm sure you know this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned this document in your submission, but to what purpose? What were you trying to demonstrate through this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is similar to the previous document. First of all, this was an issue pertaining to the international conflict, and this gentleman is the military attache in Croatia and he's taking troops to take them to Bosnia and Herzegovina, all the while the alleged joint criminal enterprise is at play against that same people. And it says here, or rather, the president of the state says: "Pursuant to Articles 94 and 99 of the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia and in keeping with the conclusion of the parliament issued on the 27th of March," which means that the parliament of the Republic of Croatia reached a conclusion and the government issued a proposal on the 6th of April, by which they bound Franjo Tudjman to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina. Franjo Tudjman was not the one who issued decisions on the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina; it was the parliament. And the document is important because the -- there were already allegations in the indictment about the joint criminal enterprise. If you recognise a state, if [as interpreted] you recognise its territorial integrity and everything else -- and now -- well, can you -- could you imagine that degree of cunning and craftiness pursuant to which we will first recognise a state and then we will cut off its face. I don't have any comment to that. The way somebody's mind worked in order to reach such conclusions is just beyond me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I will now address a new topic. I will be talking about sniping. Now, my personal analysis of this, and of course it's my own and each and everyone can have its own opinion, but my own analysis of the situations that any casualty -- when there's a casualty of sniping the criminal judge must -- in order to find the responsibility must make sure that he knows where the shot came from. If this trier of fact cannot ascertain for sure where the shot came from, there will always be doubt as to where it actually came from, as to the origin of the shot. In the past as a professional Judge, I had to deal with this problem -- also when I was a prosecutor. And in my personal experience, I must say that when you have a casualty that was shot at, you must absolutely know exactly where the shot came from, where it originated, and who was holding the weapon. That's the only way that you can correctly find the responsible person. So personally I selected seven victims who were shot at when you were commander of the HVO between June, July, and November. We need to save time, of course, you know I have really scrutinised this very carefully previously, and I will give you the main details of the cases and you will comment on this inasmuch, of course, as you have knowledge of all this. First incident on July 27, 1993, the victim was Arif Gosto. He was shot in the lower part of his leg while he was helping the fire brigade put out a fire in the Saric Harem cemetery. According to him it was well-known that HVO snipers were shooting from the Stotina plateau. According to the OTP expert, Mr. Patrick van der Weijden, the range of the tier and the type of wound seemed to suggest that the calibre of the munition -- of the weapon used could be very well a sniping weapon, 7.62 millimetres, 51 millimetre, 7.62 -- 54 millimetre -- or 792 R -- minus R. So it seems that the shot originated from the Stotina plateau. What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say the date is the 27 June 1993, when I wasn't down there. That's the first thing I have to say. And secondly, I did not have the time to analyse this case in great depth, or rather, I didn't do it for a simple reason. I did not have all the element which would either confirm or show that this is impossible like I did in some other cases. And my general objection would be as follows. The 600- or 7 00-metre distances, Your Honours, would require two men as sharpshooters, the gun should be very well calibrated. The distance is so far that it would take a super professional -- I don't know whether you ever held a rifle and tried to target something at a 600-metre distance. Did you ever see how objects move if you move your sighting device by just a millimetre. In any case, this was on the 27th of June, I wasn't there, I can't talk about it, and I did not have enough elements at my disposal to completely refute this allegation as I did with others, with similar ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second incident, second victim, the name is Omer Dilberovic, it happened on August 30th, 1993, it's a Muslim who lived in the Pasica [phoen] area of East Mostar. He was hit in the right leg when he was just crossing an open space, a 20-metre-long open space in Mazulidjice [phoen]. This victim said that he heard the detonation of the bullet and that the bullet came from the western side of Mostar, but he cannot really say where the shot originated from. According to the expert the shot came from the Ledara building located 677 -- 677 metres from where the victim was. According to the expert, this is the building that gives the best view of the site where the incident occurred, and according to the expert, the sharpshooter was in the higher floors -- the upper floors. What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that this is absurd. Maybe you could -- well, the first distance is 700 metres. The person climbed the Ledara building, and did not show precisely how you can actually see the place from the Ledara, but, Your Honours, could I please place this part on the ELMO, this part here? Can I show this part here, please? Here you can see the direction of movement, the victim's movement. The bullet came from here and hit the victim in the right upper leg from this direction. And now could you please look at the photo of the place where the victim was. You can't see the two roads here which you can see in the drawing. Let's put the two images on the ELMO at the same time. So this is the place where the victim was hit. Where is this man going? Is he going from here? From there? Where is Ledara? Is he going down the road? Why is he walking by the houses? I don't -- I can't see where this person is moving to and from. We don't have any elements that would establish his movement, although I have come up with a possible variant. Since Ledara is very high up, I looked at the wound, there should be a gap between the entry and exit wound which you can't see on the victim's legs. See, he took a shot of the place but he didn't show the movement, he didn't show any directions. Where is the victim going on this road? Where is Ledara? This is something, the sketch does not correspond to the photo which is supposed to depict the same place. And this is not how you do things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking for this drawing to be admitted? Yes. Let's give it a number.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've already tendered all the sketches under my expert's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move to the third incident, September 7, 1993, the victim's name is Alija Jakupovic, it's a fireman. He was hit in the back of the skull while he was driving the fire truck after having put out a fire. He was crossing an open space that was about 100 to 150 metres long in Street -- in Lakisica Street. We know, according to Elmer Demic, who was another fireman in Mostar, that the shots hit the fire truck as well as the driver of the fire truck. And according to Elmer Demic, the shots came from white buildings shaped -- from Centre 2 that was located in the west of Mostar. It was a number of high-rises of different levels. The expert says that this incident might have been caused by the use of the calibres I mentioned earlier. According to him, the shot probably originated from the Ledara building. There was about 786 metres from where the victim was located. He believes that the sharpshooter was in the upper floors of this Ledara building. General Praljak, what's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that you shouldn't provide your thoughts in an expert opinion. You have to provide your claims and you have to prove them. First, there is a discrepancy between the statement of the victim, who says that he is from the city and the expert who says that that came from Ledara. Maybe, maybe, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak, you are saying things that are not correct. You are saying to us, Your Honour, you have to prove your claims, you have to prove them. We do not have to prove anything. It is the Prosecutor that proves and we are just here to see who in the end has succeeded in proving them. Maybe it's a problem of translation or transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There might have been a problem in the translation into English because in French it is not what I heard. Mr. Praljak, what did you say exactly? You didn't mention the Judges, did you, because I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you. I said the expert must not use in his expert report "I think" and there shouldn't be a discrepancy between the victim, who says this came from some buildings; and the expert, who says that this is from Ledara. But let's look at the previous photo, there is a road on which the fire brigade truck is moving and this shot was taken from the possible place from which the shot came. This is the sketch. This is how the fire brigade truck is moving and it comes at 90 degrees vis-à-vis the direction of movement and you can see it here. And what happened, the bullet pierced the last -- the back window and the man was wounded in the back of his head. How did this happen? If I'm sitting like this and if I'm moving in the direction of Judge Trechsel, if the shot comes from here, how can it hit me here? And this is what the person drew. He says the bullet came from here, the witness, and the photo we saw we can see that the back window was pierced and we can see that the back of the victim's head was hit. Maybe there's some bullets that make a curved trajectory, but this would be illogical nonsense and it is really sad that an expert is allowed to draw something like this. You see, the bullet is supposed to come from here, the vehicle is moving in this direction, here's the vehicle, and this bullet which was apparently shot from here hit him in the back of the head. And if you were looking at the window that was broken, you really can't draw such a conclusion. What the expert is claiming here is nothing short of stupidity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now move to another victim, but it's a protected witness so I will not mention any names. This occurred on September 29, 1993, Witness DB. He is hit on the right shoulder blade by a sniper while he was -- he is hit while he was trying to help someone - I'm not going to mention the name of the other person that will help identify him - but he's shot by a sniper while he's trying to help someone that was also -- had already been shot by a sniper. This happened in the Brkica Street, about 50 metres from the fire station. This is on page 13.014 and 13.015. This is the testimony, but the victim was not able to be certain where the shots came from. The place -- you have no view of any place the shot might come from when you are located where the victim was hit, but this -- he was close to the Spanish square. So the shot might have originated from any place around this Spanish square because all of the roads about this Brkica Street make a tunnel which limits the possibility of shooting. According to the expert, the most possible place the shooting might have occurred is 1-metre-80-high platform located among the trees on the western side of the Spanish square about 600 metres from where the incident occurred. And the expert concludes, therefore, that the shot probably originated from this platform. When he went on site he says that he actually saw the platform, it was still erected. Apparently he even climbed on this platform and from there he had view on the place where the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No photos were taken and that platform -- he never asked himself whether that platform existed during the conflict. Second of all, I enclosed a series of photos which clearly depict that from that platform you could not see the place that he describes in his report, and not even a crazy man in Spanish square on a separation line could shoot from a platform. This is one absurd after another. We're talking about a 750-metre distance and a man on a platform. You can't see a thing from that platform. I took tens of photos from that platform in the direction of the -- of opposing side. The Spanish square was the place of fierce combat between the HVO and the BiH army, and to have somebody on that platform shooting at a distance of 750 metres and you can't see a thing from there -- he never even tried to take a photo to see whether there was any visibility. These are two pages of the same piece of evidence, the sketch here and the explanation arises from there, it could be this, it could be that, it could be other. I really -- I don't know. I'm claiming -- but let's cut this long story short. I'm claiming that from the platform you could not see that place. I'm claiming as well that - and this can be checked, this can be verified, I hope that you can, I don't know whether you can at all send somebody down there to take any shots. Maybe the Prosecutor can check. I did my check and I enclosed my photos. You can't see the place where the thing allegedly happened from the platform. Second of all, from a platform that was not there, nobody could shoot from there because that was the time of the conflict because the Prosecutor or expert claims that there may have been a tree there, but if you're standing in a tree and you are shooting at somebody, that person you're shooting at can lower you down from that tree as if you were a monkey, and this is not what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... incident of September 29, 1993, the victim's name is Damir Katica who was 14 at the time. His friend Neno Mackic -- he had a friend Neno Mackic, and they were shot several times when they were both crossing street Orucevica Sokak in the Donja Mahala area. According to Damir Katica, the shots came from a house located on the Stotina hill. This house was the only place possible that the shots could come from. It was well-known that snipers used this house to shoot from in Stotina. When he testified he said that the tree and the house that had a satellite dish and that are in between this house and Stotina and the place the incident occurred was much smaller at the time, so the house and the tree were much smaller at the time. And he says that this house was controlled by HVO. Now, the expert says the following. He says the house is 470 metres from where the victim was shot. General Praljak, what can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the sketch here made by the expert. The boy is moving in this direction. The shot comes from this direction, this is Orucevica Street. This is the spot where the boy was hit, right in the middle of this road here. And we have seen from the statements that the road is wide. You can see here, Your Honours, this is the arrow marked by the expert on the photograph. This is the narrow street, it's about 5, 5 and a half metres wide. So at the middle, having passed 2 and a half metres running, the boy was hit from a distance of 487 metres. Let us move on -- well, this is a sketch that I made. This is Stotina, this is the movement of the boy. This is where he's standing, and this is the direction in which he's moving. Then I also made some calculations here. 480 metres, the boy is running 4 metres per second, he's 14 to 15 years of age, these are standard values, and for a bullet, 7.62 or any similar, to pass 470 metres, it takes 0.7 seconds once the bullet leaves the muzzle. And at this rate of speed, the boy takes 0.5 seconds to run 2 metres. So he would already be here in 0.5 seconds if you take a normal way in which a boy runs. So there's no targeting. There's just firing. The bullet leaving the muzzle, flying through the air, it takes 0.7 seconds for this whole procedure, and the boy was hit after 0.5 seconds because he was hit when he passed 2 and a half metres. So he was hit before the bullet actually reached him. Well, we've seen this here. This is the front side, this is where the bullet entered the body. Now, we were shown this. If you're running in this direction and the bullet is coming from this direction, how is it possible that he is hit here, here? If I'm running towards you from here and the bullet is coming from the left-hand side, how can I then be hit here, and so on and so forth? So he was hit from the direction in which he was running. He was running in this direction and he was hit from the same direction, and he had hit him here and exited in the back. Secondly, Stotina, even if we were to speculate now is 60 or 70 metres elevated, and the entry and exit wounds are completely straight. It's level, and even if we were to speculate, the bullet should have entered further up from the exit wounds. I should have made a calculation as to the number of centimetres, but I don't want to burden you with that. These are just speculations. So if you want to, please look at this. 500 metres, that's five large football stadiums -- football pitches. If you run across a street of that size which is this wide, a sniper should observe this person, notice this person, target, fire, and hit in a very short period of time. Well, I don't know what conclusions you can draw, but nothing of the sort can be done except in maybe science fiction novels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last-but-one incident. On 10th October, 1993, Munib Klaric, he lives in West Mostar. He was hit in the heel by sniper fire whilst he was fetching water in the Neretva River. He was in Podharemi in Mejdan in East Mostar in front of the steps that end the Kusalova Street and he's backed with his back to the Neretva River and to the Stotina hill. He believes that the fire originated from Stotina because of the positions of the entry and exit wound and because the sharpshooter was positioned on Stotina with a clear line of sight on to the position where he was wounded. As to the expert, he says that the most likely place is the house which is 449 metre away from the position where the victim was. What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, similar as before. Here is the sketch, this is the Neretva. There is an area here. There are stairs here. And this is the trajectory of the bullet fired from Stotina. Well, please look at this. We'll now see what -- well, the photographs that were shown to us, how the man was positioned at the time when he was hit. So the bullet is supposed to come from this direction. The angle is 30 degrees -- well, that's 90 degrees, that would be 30 degrees in relation to this building, so a 30-degree angle laterally. The bullet comes from the side. Look at the entry wound from the above. The exit wound is down here, just below the heel, and I calculated that the angle here is 45 degrees. So we have a man standing here, facing in this direction. His heel is facing the Neretva. The bullet hits him, according to the expert report, at an angle of 30 degrees in relation to his body. The bullet enters his heel from above and exits at an angle of 45 degrees on the underside of the heel, and I simply cannot understand it, to be quite frank. I put in all the angles here in an effort to show how this man might have been standing. So this bullet, it was probably -- it had probably been fired in the air, and the descending trajectory -- in its descending trajectory the bullet can be deadly, but there's not a chance that this kind of a wound is caused by a bullet coming from this direction, a bullet that would then exit on the underside of the heel at that angle. It's quite clear, but we should perhaps do some forensic medical expert analyses, but the way this expert did it, I asked him whether he was he ashamed and he said he was not. But I am embarrassed for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last witness -- but earlier on, regarding the first witness I had said that it was on the 27th of July, inside, and you spoke about the 27th of June. I checked the 92 bis statement by this witness. He said it happened on the 27th of July, so he may have been wrong but in his statement he spoke about the 27th of July. As to the last witness, it happened on the 30th of October -- or last victim, rather, 30th of October, 1993, Enver Dziho and Stojan Kacic, they were the victims. Enver Dziho was hit when he was crossing Ali Sekitar [phoen] Street near the Razvitak building. As to Stojan Kacic, he was a paramedic and he was hit in the leg when he was transporting Dziho, who had been wounded, right up to the ambulance. So there's a first victim, Dziho, and a second victim, the ambulance man who was carrying him. According to a resident of Mostar, Dzemal Barakovic, he was the driver of the fire brigade, he thinks that the bullet hitting Kacic came from the green building located at the Spanish square. The expert said that high-rise buildings are likely positions for sniper fire. In this case the green building is located 743 metres away from the place where the victims were. According to the expert, although this is a large distance, 743 metres, it is a possible distance for a marksman who is competent and well equipped. So what do you have to say this before the break?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've lined up all the photographs here. If you recall, I asked the victim, Please tell me, sir, do you still wonder where the bullet that hit you was fired from, and he said, Yes, General. At the place, at the spot, where these two people were wounded, it is impossible -- you cannot have the line of vision, line of sight, from the western side of Mostar, from the glass house or anywhere else. And here the expert even provided the wrong photograph, a false photograph, indicating that there is line of sight when there isn't any. But we have quite specific and concrete documents. It is impossible to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I won't have any more questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, huh -- well, look at the sketch. This building is supposed to be in this direction, the direction from which the bullet came. He made the photograph here, view of the Spanish square -- well, nobody knows what this is. Here he showed a building that has nothing to do with the glass house, glass building, that makes no sense. These are probably some balconies on the hotel. This here, what he drew in, has nothing to do with the place of the incident because this old building is not there in the street. This is all a lie, a deceiving lie, and you can see here it says, "A view from the platform on the Spanish square." I don't know what view it is, but this has nothing to do with the actual view of the spot. Let us move on. Your Honour, this is the spot where the incident took place. This is the Marsala Tita Square, the Razvitak building is here, here. And where do you see the building that was shown by the Prosecutor? Look, this is Razvitak. It's a totally different part of Mostar. This is an attempt to deceive you. This is what you can see from the spot of the incident facing west. This is an old building in Mostar, another photograph of the same scene where they were hit. This is the firefighters' hall. Let us move on. Now, of course, Your Honours, I took close-ups. This is the Bristol Hotel which completely obscures the view now even closer. There's nothing in the back that you can see. This is the Spanish square. This is the secondary school. This is the boulevard. Now we're facing east, slowly turning eastwards. This is what you can see from the Spanish square in a direction -- well, this is what we would see if we looked east from the platform. This is where the demarcation lines were. Now let us look at the glass building which is not on the square itself. Just a moment. This is what you can see on the Spanish square, again if you're facing east. This is the platform that in his opinion could be used to fire from -- well, look at it, please. This was probably done for some kind of a performance. I put a man here up on the ladder. This is the man that I asked to go up there so that I could photograph him, and then I went up there and I had a look at -- had a look eastwards to see what is it that you can actually see. Please look, well it's absolutely -- okay, so this is a close-up using a different objective. This is the Marsala Tita Bridge, and the street goes left here and it is only further down that it reaches the fire brigade hall. An even greater close-up, and so on and so forth. You can just go down there and check it. This man tried to make all of you fools -- all of us fools. And this is completely impermissible for an international Tribunal. This Tribunal tried to save some people, but instead they should have put them in jail for this kind of thing. In normal courts, in national courts, such people are tried for contempt of court or attempts to pervert the course of justice and they are convicted and punished. That is my opinion. You can check any claim that I made on the ground and you can take me with you, in handcuffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions. The Trial Chamber would like to know approximately how much time you're going to use. Mr. Karnavas, you're going to be the first to speak, so what is the likely time you're going to need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. To be very frank, I don't know the -- with any degree of exactitude, therefore I would say that I would prefer to have all of my time available to myself. I will try to be as expeditious as possible, however. I'm not sure I quite answered the question, but suffice it to say, I will take the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning. I also think that I will need all the time that I have been allotted. I believe that at the beginning of my examination I will petition the Court to allot any remaining time proportionately to me, if any is left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that you had been given 20 hours divided in five, that's four hours per Defence team. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning. I believe that six hours would be sufficient for the General Petkovic Defence to deal with some topics with General Praljak, and I believe that with this request for additional time that we have submitted we can fit in within the time-frame the time that is allotted to the Defence. And if any time remains, we would also like to get our portion of the remaining time if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are asking for additional time. I haven't heard of any motion to the effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have not made any requests for additional time because this is the first time that we are stating the time that we would want to have, but as far as I could understand from my colleagues that are preparing for the cross-examination, we believe that with the additional time that we would then get we could fit in. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As my colleagues, I hope and I will do my best to complete my examination in the time that has been allotted to me, the four hours, if you divide the 20 hours; but if I fail to do so and if there is any time remaining, I would also like to participate proportionately in the use of that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Well, nobody has spoken to me about any re-distribution of time. If we decide to examine Mr. Praljak, we will probably need just one session and all the time that we haven't -- we'll have not used -- well, it's up to the Court to decide what to do with that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a break. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave I would like to say what I've established with regard to document P 06020, which is a report by Mr. Emil Harah dated 23rd October 1993. I said about that document that this document has been forged, and everything I'm going to say I have already run by Mr. Stringer so there's not going to be any discord among the two -- between the two of us. Can we please go into private session because I'm going to be talking about protected witnesses, whose names I would still like to mention in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I saw you waving a document based, apparently, on the 1991 census in the area of Travnik and in the central area. Do you seek to tender the document? We can give you an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, an I C number for the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This document shall be given Exhibit IC01031. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, please show the document to Mr. Stringer in case he has any objections to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We don't object to its admission, Your Honour. We, of course, reserve the right to challenge its correctness. Mr. President, could I make one brief remark in response to what my learned friend Ms. Alaburic has just said. I don't think we need to go back into private session, and just to indicate that what counsel said is correct in terms of -- and obviously the Trial Chamber can go back and see Witness EA. In her earlier intervention Ms. Alaburic indicated that Witness EA testified that the document was a forgery. That was technically incorrect because he said he didn't know, he hadn't seen it and he would not say whether it was or was not. However, as counsel's correctly indicated, there's an earlier witness statement, the 92 bis statement from a different witness, which does claim that the document is a forgery. My only sort of qualification is at the very end counsel indicated that the Prosecution would agree or share the view that the document was a forgery, and I think in light of the testimony from both of the witnesses or the evidence from both of the witnesses I think it's ultimately for the Trial Chamber to make that decision. The Prosecution was putting it to Witness EA that it was a forgery. The witness declined to accept that suggestion. He did say that he had, in fact, ordered the reporting or reporting as was indicated in the exhibit so that there is some -- there is some degree of corroboration, if you will. But I wouldn't want to accept that the Prosecution now shares the view that it's a forgery. I think that the record is complete on this and that it's ultimately for the Trial Chamber to assign whatever weight it wants to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is now on record. I'll ask my colleagues whether they have questions themselves. No questions for Judge Mindua, for Judge Prandler, or for Judge Trechsel. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor. You have given us your documents. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon -- or good morning, again, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Before I begin I do want to make one observation in light of what I just heard from the Prosecution. It is my understanding when a party, Prosecution or Defence, puts something to the witness, it is based on a good-faith basis because it's an allegation in a sense. So I would not quite share the liberal interpretation of the way it was put, but I'll leave that for another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Now, if I could have your undivided attention, I'm going to be moving rather quickly, initially through just some housekeeping matters, I would say, and I'm going to be referring to the transcripts at time. S. O let's start off with the issue of June 30th, 1993, Judge Antonetti on page 41.602 made references to some documents, one in particular that was authored by Siljeg, Mr. Siljeg. And so with that I would like to point -- direct your attention to P 03026, P 03026. We've seen this document before. This is a document that was shown to you by President Antonetti, and I'm going to direct your attention first to the very first line because that's something that caught everyone's attention where it says - this would be on page 2, Your Honours, of the English version - it says: "Brado was familiarised with the report from Mostar with a conversation between A. Pasalic and S. Halilovic, and with the command issued by the head of the defence department and president of the HVO HB HZB based on the following is requested ..." Now, my focus is where it says "with the command issued by," and it would give the impression that my client, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, was actually issuing commands. Was a command issued by Dr. Jadranko Prlic to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you know at any time -- at any point in time whether Dr. Prlic was issuing commands to anyone, including -- or I should say especially to Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that while I was in command he never issued an order to me or any of my subordinates, as far as I know. I'm sure about myself, and as for the others I never heard, nobody ever informed me that he would have issued a lower-ranking commander with an order of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, sticking with this subject if we could go to P 03038, and in conjunction with this document we'll be looking at P 03039, Your Honours. So if you have both of them handy. If we look at P 03038, we see it's dated 30 June 1993. We see a number, number 02-1-765/93. Now, as I understand it, the first part of this particular document is a proclamation until you get to the bottom part where some sort of an order is being issued to that effect to a certain extent, it would be the second page on your document. But let's look at the first part. Is this an order or a proclamation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a proclamation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at the next page where it does say that: "Pursuant to the authorisation and the new situation, the head of the HVO HZ HB defence department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, issues the following order ..." When we look at the order this is not an operational order, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at the next document which is P 03039 and we look at where it says "subject," we can see the number, order number, and of course it goes to Mr. Siljeg. And we see -- and we compare the contents, essentially the order is the same, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we've agreed that this again is not an operational order, in the sense that neither Dr. Jadranko Prlic nor Mr. Bruno Stojic are issuing operational orders to Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Siljeg says precisely that this is a message.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for those of us who may have forgotten what happened on and about that particular day, is it not a fact that that was after -- it was around that time when there was an incident that caught everyone's attention?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an incident, Mr. Karnavas. It was a treason and aggression. It was high treason, that's what this could have been considered, because the HVO fighters of Muslim ethnicity attacked their comrades-in-arms according to a pre-designed plan. They disarmed them, they killed many, and the BiH army on that day launched an open aggression against the Croatian Defence Council. You can't call this an incident, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I apologise. I'm trying to be as neutral as I can so the evidence comes from you rather than me, even though this is cross-examination. Now, I'm going to stick with this period for right now, so if we could look at some documents that precede this period and then follow that period because there is an issue before the Court concerning reverse ethnic cleansing. And so if I could direct your attention to 1D 01668, 1D 01668. This is a document we've seen before, and they are minutes from a meeting. And we can see the agenda, the very first item on the agenda, it talks about the head of the department -- the defence department. It says: "In his report he said that the Muslim forces were carrying out coordinated attacks in Central Bosnia and northern Herzegovina to seize areas ... which according to the Vance-Owen Plan were intended to be included in the areas with the majority Croatian authority (provinces 8 and 10), continued to isolate, terrorise, and destroy everything that is Croatian. In the general area of Travnik, in the municipalities of Kiseljak, Vitez, Vares, and the municipalities of Konjic and Jablanica, as well as in locations where Croats are the minority population, (for example, in Sarajevo, Zenica, Tuzla), the survival of every single Croat and the Croatian people as a whole is seriously threatened." And my he question to you, sir, at this point in time, does this accurately reflect what was happening on that location on or about the middle of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at page 3 in the English where we have conclusions - I don't know the exact page, I'll give it to you in a second - it would be page 3. If we look at the conclusions, you see that there is a -- proposal was made to the Presidency of the HZ HB and the supreme commander of the HVO to urgently request military assistance from the Republic of Croatia to protect the Croats in BH. Now, we already know who the Presidency was and just once more the supreme commander of the HVO was who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
