utterances.text: And now if we look at the next conclusion he says: "A proposal was made to the Presidency of the HZ HB and the HVO supreme commander to adopt a decision to pull out all military units from areas outside the designated Croatian provinces, together with the Croatian inhabitants living there. To this effect, demand cooperation and assistance from UNPROFOR and UNHCR." Question: Given that -- given your position and your understanding of the events, can you please explain to us why such a conclusion was being proposed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because -- well, while there was an ongoing aggression by the BiH army against the HVO, in the areas under the control of the BH army there was about 15 to 18.000 HVO soldiers fighting under the command of the BiH army which had been agreed in advance, which means that in one area of Bosnia and Herzegovina the BiH army launched an operation to conquer the areas inhabited by Croats, it attacked the HVO, whereas there is another area where the HVO together with the BiH army set out to defend the territory from the Serbs. It was not an easy fact to accept or support. That's why the proposal was worded as you see it, but it was never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then if we look at number 5 it said: "Issue a special proclamation to volunteers from the Republic of Croatia and the emigre community to enlist in the HVO to defend Croatian areas in BH." Now, General Praljak, isn't it a fact that Herzegovinians, Croat Herzegovinians, went to Croatia when initially Croatia was attacked by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, over 13.000 -- at least 13.000 fought in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it the Herzegovina -- President Tudjman as well as the Croatian army at the time, such as it was or being developed relied on the Croatian Herzegovinians to defend Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were good fighters in the Croatian army because we had a very high level of national awareness. We were Croatian patriots of the entire nation, not only of some isolated regions or some such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And isn't it a fact, General Praljak, that many of those volunteers that went there stayed there and one of the reasons that you had these sorts of conclusions was to get some of those volunteers to come back, those who had volunteered to go fight for Croatia now to come back and now defend their own villages and cities; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact, very few returned, unfortunately, for all sorts of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the next document, 1D 02309. Now, we're going to actually July 1, 1993, sticking again with our theme about that period of time. Here we have a letter from Mile Akmadzic, he came in and testified, and we can see at the very top, to the Secretary-General of the United Nations, to the chairman of the Security Council of the UN, to the chairmen of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia. And here he talks about the events of June 30th, 1993. If you look at this could you please tell us whether, first of all, Mr. Akmadzic's account is accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you tell us now whether anybody from the UN came to do an investigation and see what exactly had happened? Did they send somebody, some commission, anybody to see what would happen to the Croats that were slain by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The reporting continued in a totally erroneous and false way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, P 03413, now we're -- it's a little bit beyond this period. This is dated 13 July 1993, and we see over here there's a conclusion of the HVO HZ HB reached on 15th of June, 1993, I don't know what the -- yeah, and it says: "The Croatian people in Central Bosnia and Northern Herzegovina are under threat of massacre and extermination. Muslim units in the area are many times stronger and their strength is increasing by the hour. Therefore, if we do not undertake the appropriate measures, exodus of the Croatian people from those areas and their ancestral homes will be inevitable ..." And I won't go on, but can you please tell us whether indeed that was the situation as described by Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, there are some proposals down here, but can you please tell us whether the UN sent any forces there to prevent any massacres occurring or any atrocities occurring against the Croats in Central Bosnia in and around that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody wanted to write or hear about that. Nobody wanted to know. Nobody cared, and there were persistent claims that the HVO was attacking somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. I do not wish to interrupt you because I know how unpleasant it is to be interrupted when you want to sort of highlight something, but my question goes along the same lines. General Praljak, you referred on several occasions to the fact that I had presided over another trial in which Muslim generals were tried. We now have an official and public judgement of the trial proceedings. In Guca Gora, the Croatian population had fled from Guca Gora, I remember, although there was not even one BH army soldier. They had fled because they were terrorised, and then only later did the Mujahedin arrive. But when they arrived there was no one left, everybody had left. So what did you find? Do you think that this was a rather frequent event in Croatian villages because of rumour, because they'd heard that something had happened 10 or 20 kilometres away from there? Did that cause the population to leave because they were afraid, and understandably so? Did you witness this sort of thing, recurrent event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew of such cases. It was not always necessary -- or rather, there were two possible options, or maybe even three. The military fled because it had been defeated and it was followed by the population; or the population fled before the military and the HVO would then have nothing to defend and then they would leave; and the third option was this, where there was no HVO protection, they fled in fear. Fear is a justified feeling. If 3 kilometres away somebody kills somebody else or ten people are killed or somebody's decapitated, the fear grows out of proportion and people tried to flee for their dear life to avoid getting massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before I ask my next question, General Praljak, if it would be of assistance, we could take your binder and give you the documents one by one if that would help. I leave it to you. Would that be of assistance? My colleague Ms. Tomanovic could assist me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And picking up just at one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, as you're speaking about the binder, can you explain whether at all there is any logic in the way the documents are? Because I failed to detect that. It's also rendered more difficult that sometimes you have "EXH" in front but I have not found any reason for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. My apologies, Your Honour. To be honest -- the exhibits, I'm told, are marked specifically. The order, I must apologise, I was working -- I was working throughout the night to sort of accommodate the time allotted to me plus the way the proceedings are going, and then it wasn't until this very -- the session this morning that I re-arranged my own, trying to figure out where I'm going. But I will -- I think we'll -- I think we'll be able to move along rather quickly and I'll be slower with the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. And if you can give a hint, this is the next number but it is not following immediately, it's on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please understand also and be sure that this is to assist you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- and your client so that we can fully follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- but picking up where Judge Antonetti left off, because we will be talking about the Mujahedin, but as I understand it, they were primarily located in and around Zenica; is that correct? That's where they were headquartered?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were there, but they were employed in a much wider area, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But I -- and I take it Zenica was under constant threat and attack, either by the Croats or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Against Croats? What?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was Zenica the sort of place that required the Mujahedin to be there for the protection of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my point. Can you think of any reason why, then, you had this huge number of foreign fighters stationed in a place where they were not required when the fighting against the Serbs, at least, were in other places?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those men as part of a wider policy appeared in Bosnia and Herzegovina much more to the purpose of spreading Islam than to the purpose of being engaged in a defence war for the benefit of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They wanted to spread Islam and train people for further activities across Europe and the world. Their primary goal was not to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And at that time Sarajevo was still under siege?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I understand, and we'll get to it, at one point you had encouraged Izetbegovic to assist in the liberation of Sarajevo, but he basically did not want to have that discussion with you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not want to have that discussion. I believe that he never, ever seriously wanted to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. There were two operations which seemingly were meant to lift the blockade of Sarajevo; however, the way they were planned and the forces, the little forces that were used, give rise to the belief that there was no real intent behind them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's one of the reasons I asked. You offered to assist in deblocking - this was in 1992, as I understand it, when Izetbegovic came to the Mostar area - you offered to deblock -- to assist in the deblocking of Sarajevo. But it begs the question, a question that hasn't been asked in this courtroom: Why aren't the Mujahedin in Sarajevo trying to deblock Sarajevo? Why have them in Zenica where there is nothing there to defend, because Zenica is more or less protected? Why have them there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the question in that it invites the witness to speculate about something he doesn't have personal knowledge about, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the General -- first of all, we're talking to a general who served. So if he doesn't know, who would? I think in light of his involvement in and around the area, he's meeting with Halilovic, he's meeting with other military commanders, why -- how is it that he's not capable of rendering an opinion? And I've already laid down the foundation. Zenica doesn't need protection, yet there you have the Mujahedin running around. You know, they don't -- they're not needed there. Sarajevo is under attack, and as the general indicated, it might be because Izetbegovic's plan was to have his own people get killed in order to play the victim, in order to get the international community to try to come in, because as we heard and was written by Mr. Owen, he wanted the internationals to come in and get involved in the fighting. So he was sacrificing his own people as -- as we will go along is because he had intentions of establishing an Islamic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, now the theory of -- the conspiracy theory continues to expand, but it doesn't answer the basic objection, which is that the witness is being invited to speculate on a theory of the Defence. It's a theory they can make, but it's more for later and it's not really for this witness because he doesn't know anything about that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Your Honour. I'll rephrase it. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment because there may be within the Trial Chamber some disagreement on the issue. I have to turn to my fellow Judges to see whether you're allowed to continue in this vein, so I'm going to talk with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After discussing the matter, the Trial Chamber is of the view that one should avoid speculations. There is agreement on this. Secondly, the Trial Chamber is of the view that the witness can explain why the Mujahedin were in Zenica because there must be some military reason for it. So militarily was their presence there legitimate or not? It could be an interesting issue. But personally let me add this, let me add this to the Trial Chamber's ruling, personally in the other trial proceedings I had an opportunity to ask the very same question as the one put by Mr. Karnavas. I asked a witness how it was that the 3rd Corps with 130.000 men did nothing to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. Those who know all about the case file can legitimately ask themselves that question, and I'd asked a witness why nothing had been done to move to Sarajevo rather than to launch an attack in Central Bosnia. There may be reasons, specific reasons for that. So, please, Mr. Karnavas, do try to focus your questions on facts and do avoid speculation as much as you can because automatically this is going to raise objections by the Prosecution and we will have to settle the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Staying with this topic, do you know whether any of the Mujahedin were redeployed to Sarajevo to try to deblock Sarajevo during this period? That's a factual question I think that you can certainly give an answer to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not. But I am a witness, now I'm speaking as a witness. I spoke to Mr. Izetbegovic in the autumn of 1992. At the time we were strong. The HVO had some victories behind it and it was strong. And I proposed that we lift the siege of Sarajevo jointly, and Mr. Izetbegovic said in diplomatic terms that, No, no, the international community would intervene. And I told him, Look, you have 5.000 people dead already. And if they did not intervene after 5.000 deaths that means they would not intervene at all. And he again refused and he said, Well, they'll intervene. So the correct conclusion is that Mr. Izetbegovic - and this is what I'm saying, this is my conclusion, not your conclusion - that he was hoping that because the Serbs were shelling Sarajevo and there is a lot of casualties, that this would create a critical mass in the world public opinion and that the international community would intervene. I maintained that it would not. I was proven right. And I still maintain. It's not only the Mujahedin but also the elite Muslim units, the 7th, 17th, and so on, the whole of the 3rd Corps and elements of the 1st Corps that were outside of Sarajevo never took any serious action to deblock Sarajevo. This is not just some rumour or anything; this is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll leave that for now and I want to go back to where we were because we were talking about that period of June/July. But now I'm going to move to November 1993, staying with the topic of reverse ethnic cleansing because now we're going to look at 1D 01269 and 1D 01270, we'll look at them together. So 1D 01269, 1D 01270. And the first document, 1D 01269, we can see is dated 4 November 1993. If we look at the bottom of the page we see that it's signed by Franjo Komarica. At the top we see that he is the bishop of Banja Luka. And for those who may have forgotten, Banja Luka is within the Republika Srpska at the time, Serb-occupied territory; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is the same bishop who was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize because throughout the war he refused to leave Banja Luka and chose to stay there to try to protect the Croats that were living in and around the Banja Luka area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if -- it would appear, if we look at this, that Mr. Komarica is either trying to get assistance to help Croats who are trapped or he too is engaged in a joint criminal enterprise as a member or he is at least aiding and abetting because this would be providing substantial assistance, it could be concluded, by asking for help, urgent help, to get these Croats out of the area. Can you please tell us, if you know, based on your experience, your knowledge at the time, whether what Bishop Komarica is describing in this letter, are these accurate facts or is this flight of fancy, simply to promote reverse ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are accurate facts, and if we had enough time for you to look at a film depicting the looting, the pillage of Vares by the 7th Muslim Brigade after it entered the town, then you would see what it looked like. Here there is a request for 3 tonnes of diesel, this is the cooperation with the Serbs, the fuel was needed for the buses to take the people out. The plan to attack Vares was drafted a long time before the events in Stupni Do and it started -- it all started a long time before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And it appears that what he is suggesting here -- he's asking the president of the HVO HZ HB to provide some resources, if we can call it that, to the Serb side in order to -- for this evacuation to occur; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, they needed fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was there any other way for those people that were trapped to leave the area without at least getting some sort of outside help?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just one final question. Do you believe that Bishop Komarica, who stayed there, stayed with his flock, if you will, in the middle of the war, you knowing him because you did testify to that earlier on direct examination, is he the sort of person that would be engaging in reverse ethnic cleansing of the Croats from their ancestral lands in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's inconceivable. I know the bishop, Komarica, and I know what he did later and the nomination, he was nominated with five other people to -- for the Nobel Peace Prize and this is inconceivable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to switch to another topic, just a brief one. This whole notion of the map of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, we've heard all sorts of testimony about the Banovina, we've seen maps, and there was even a question that came from the Bench that we had not shown otherwise or haven't -- hadn't proved, at least that's how I interpreted it. And so I want to just look at a couple of documents and have you discuss them a little bit. The first one is 1D 02253, 1D 02253. And then after that we will be looking at 2255, basically they're very similar in nature. If you have the document we see that this is a decision, it's dated 8 July 1992, and it says: "Pursuant to the statutory decision on temporary establishment of the executive authorities and administration in the Croatian part of Teslic municipality, the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council of Teslic-Komusina hereby adopts the following ..." And they form -- we here have a decision to form an -- administrative offices in the territory of the Croatian part of Teslic-Komusina municipality. Now -- and then if you -- and I'm not going to get into the whole debate about territory versus area because we could see it's been translated differently, the word "teritorija" is not there. But is this a geographical area that you can look and put on the map and draw a line and say this is part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which then would be part of the so-called Banovina which the Prosecution claims was being attempted to re-emerge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this had nothing to do with Banovina, nothing. If you allow me, this is a decision taken on the basis of two principles. The first is the principle of the right of any human being or a people to self-defence as the ultimate right; and this is also based on the laws in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the right and duty to organise yourselves and defend yourselves against the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But my question was more towards the geographical -- I mean -- because there seems to be this impression at least or perception that somehow we can just put all of these municipalities on a map, draw a line, and say, Here it is. This is the area that was trying to be occupied or conquered or taken or annexed away from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And that's why I wanted you to look at this decision and then we'll look at the other decision. From this decision can you -- can you conclude that there's some sort of a territory that you can carve out on the map? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as a whole. You can draw in just bits and pieces which were Croatian, but there is no whole that would coincide with Banovina or with any other kind of a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could we be assisted in getting an idea where we are talking about because I do not -- I am not familiar with this place. The name does not figure in Google maps, perhaps on the map back there, and to which municipality of Herceg-Bosna it would belong. That's what I would be interested in learning, if at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay -- if at all, I'm glad I heard the last part. Judge Trechsel, if it would be more of assistance if we could do that during the break as opposed to -- I mean, we could do that right now, but maybe during the break we could locate it on the map and then come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm all in favour of the economy of forces and time. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Because we're going to look at the next document which is 1D 02255, and this is a decision concerning Usora. And as you may recall last time there was a question, Where is Usora? And I misspoke, I indicated that it was in the Republika Srpska when in fact today it's in the Federation, and as I understand it, it's next to Doboj which is in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if you look at this decision, can you conclude that some sort of territory is being carved out that can be added on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this -- Usora was where? How big of an area are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a small area, small -- it's a small territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When we say "small" -- I mean, some may think that it's maybe, you know, a hundred square kilometres or -- how would -- what are we talking about really?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe a hundred kilometres square, 10 by 10, 10 kilometres by 10 kilometres. But, Mr. Karnavas, you can draw things in but there is no link. These are elements of the Croatian people that are simply getting organised to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina. Wherever they were they are -- they were aware of what was going on, and they were saying, Let us try to save our own lives and our homes and the state that we live in. That's what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to another topic then. We'll move rather quickly. I want to talk a little bit about this January 15, 1993, the so-called - and I underscore that "so-called" - ultimatum. Now, Judge Antonetti discussed that with you quite extensively, and you also told us the role that you played in this. But I thought it might be good to just look at a few things concerning the minutes that were -- took place at the meeting in Zagreb between Tudjman, Cyrus Vance, Lord Owen, Alija Izetbegovic, Mate Boban, on 15 January 1993, and I'm referring to P 01158, P 01158. And there's a purpose for this because later on I will take you to task as far as your generous view of Izetbegovic. Now, if we look at page 16, Your Honours, in the English version, it's the portion where we hear from Ahtisaari, who, as I understand it, recently won the Nobel Peace Prize. And here's what he's saying? And, Mr. Praljak, if you could look at -- on the bottom of the page -- or the top, it's 1 -- 01322259, that's the number. He says: "As the chairman of the Working Group, I feel bound to say something about the process we are still talking about. "It took many months for the proposals we are discussing today to come into existence and we have these proposals on the table today. "I here refer to military, constitutional, and geographical proposals or the map. "If we consider the package that is before us on the table as a whole, I think it would be fair to say that it most closely reflects the views of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina or Mr. Izetbegovic's delegation. "I think we must and it is also very important to take into account the fact that both the Muslims and Mr. Boban's delegation recognised and accepted the constitutional solutions, which has certainly, in a way, made the job easier for the co-chairmen to put more pressure on the Serbs ..." Now, let's -- and then he goes on a little bit. He talks a little bit about what President Tudjman has indicated very clearly, that there needs to be a compromise, that's on page 17, I won't read it. Then President Tudjman speaks. And then if we go, Your Honours, to page 20, we see Alija saying -- Alija Izetbegovic saying: "Let me remind you that the one item, one provision, from the papers proposed to us my Messrs. Vance and Owen stipulate and clearly state that Bosnia and Herzegovina will be a state where communication will exist, where communication between all provinces will be open ..." And then he goes on to say: "A special corridor means that Bosnia-Herzegovina will not be open, that is a mere formality in these provisions ..." And the corridor he's speaking about, is he not speaking about a corridor with the Serbs -- I mean that's a -- at least that's what he is alluding to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now let's look at what Mr. Vance says, Mr. Cyrus Vance. "Can I ask you, Mr. President, do you have any positive proposal, positive suggestions, so that we could continue working in a constructive spirit, in a constructive way?" Answer: "The aggressor should be asked to accept our proposal in its entirety with regard to the text and to accept the proposed amendments to the map. That's what he should be asked to do. In my opinion, that's a constructive approach to this question." Now, can you tell us, what sort of an answer is Alija Izetbegovic giving here? Who is the aggressor that he's speaking of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then Cyrus Vance asks him to - the next page, it would be page 22, Your Honours - he says: "Are you prepared to accept the map as it is?" And the answer is: "No." Now, you had indicated - and we're going to get to this at some point - that it was your belief that Alija Izetbegovic was a kind man, a good man, an honest man to some extent who simply was being mishandled, that he would agree to something but then the hard-liners, and you've indicated one of them was Silajdzic, at another time you said it might have been Halilovic, they were the ones that were getting him to change his mind. And I take it you still maintain that position as you provided it to us under oath during direct examination?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but you have to clarify. One thing that was sure, Mr. Karnavas, that is -- well, what Mr. Cyrus Vance is saying here, Give us your proposal, Mr. Izetbegovic. So Mr. Izetbegovic never came up with any kind of a positive proposal as to how the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina should look like. That's number one, the first fact. And secondly, well, I was nice, I was charming and I was calm, but it's also a fact that everything he signed he cancelled. Every international agreement that was signed, the signature was cancelled later on. Now, I speculated this was because he was actually run by other people --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but maybe he was also in the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- well, that's what we're going to get to, but not yet, not yet. I'm just laying the foundation, as it were. But if we go to page 28 in this particular document -- and this is where Mr. Mate Boban is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He starts on page 27, Your Honours, in your English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you look at, General Praljak, 0132-2270, here he's saying, it's very clear, on the paper at least: "When we signed the package, we knew that each of the three sides facing the Croats would not, that they would have different objections, different proposals, different -- ask for different corrections. "At any cost, one should listen to reason and make compromises and accept certain concessions in order to stop the war and make Bosnia and Herzegovina the state foreseen by Mr. Izetbegovic in his speech when he said that tomorrow it should be a free country with a free flow of people and capital. "Incompatible with his thinking is the claim that any territorial organisation means giving something to someone when Bosnia-Herzegovina is a unified whole. "Nobody can give anything to anyone, everyone has equal rights, and the rights have been determined by arguments. "And I would go back to the statement by Mr. Vance and Lord Owen when they said that we had really exhausted all arguments. We've exhausted all arguments a long time ago." And I don't want to go on, but this is Mate Boban. And to your understanding, is Mate Boban being accurate at least in his interpretation of the Vance-Owen peace process or peace plan that was being discussed at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, not only that but even the things that preceded this. So the fundamental sentence that came out of the heads of the Muslim leadership was, We are in charge here and we are here to give others something. It horrified Serbs right at the beginning, and Croats too. Who are you giving something when we actually have it, we have the right to it? And this fundament in their heads, this is the basic reason why they attacked Croats. It was all theirs. We were superfluous there. We were superfluous there. We could go to Croatia because that was our homeland and Serbs could go to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just a few more excerpts from this, if we look at page 33 - and then we're going to go on to page 34 in English and I'll give you the numbers - this is where Izetbegovic now -- and if you could look at 1 -- 01322275, Mr. Izetbegovic begins by saying he is grateful to Lord Owen for raising the question, because earlier we could see that Lord Owen is trying to move the process along, and so here is what Mr. Izetbegovic proposes. This would be on page 34. "Perhaps we should now form a mixed arbitration commission composed by you to help us resolve these problems in a just way. Mixed" -- and then he goes on: "That's the idea that first comes to my mind." So let me paint the picture, General Praljak. You have these internationals, one representative of the UN, one the EU. You have Ahtisaari there who's saying, For months we've put this proposal together, now it comes time for Izetbegovic to make a decision. And now he's saying to these international arbitrators in a sense, because that's what they're trying to do, arbitrate, he says, We should form a mixed arbitration commission, that would be useful. Now, does that sound like Izetbegovic really is interested in resolving the issue to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Again, it's calling for speculation. Anyone can read the transcript and draw conclusions and make arguments about what's being said. The General's testimony about his interpretation really isn't any more relevant than anyone else's. So obviously he can confirm or talk about factual things, but we suggest that this is irrelevant. It's not very helpful evidence, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this is why it's helpful, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me tell why it's relevant. I've sat here and I've listened to testimony and I've listened to questions from the Bench and some of the questions were concerning Mr. Izetbegovic and his personality. Now, there's going to come a time in my cross-examination where I will go through some of the General's comments about Mr. Izetbegovic's personality where he paints him in a rather generous way. And then I will show you documents and we will go into Schindler's book and we will go into the Islamic Declaration which was being waved at the SDA parties as one of their platforms, and I will show you that what really Izetbegovic had in mind was exactly what was in his "Mein Kampf," the Islamic Declaration, and that he was making trips to Iran, he was gathering -- he was building an armed force well before the HVO started, and that he had alternative motives, and that all of this is not because Izetbegovic was being mishandled by his poor brothers and sisters from his earlier days, but rather, this is Izetbegovic at the apex, he's at the very top. He is the one that authored the Islamic Declaration for which he went to jail for. And as soon as he got out, he went to Iran; as soon as he got out, he published it. And to suggest that somehow that is not part of his psyche and that's what he's trying to do is to create a Muslim state, something that he started when he was a young man when the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, not all of them but some of them, the Young Muslims, as the organisation, was collaborating with the Nazis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas, you are testify --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are telling us all this but I thought you were supposed to ask questions from a witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when somebody attacks me that I am going into an irrelevant area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, that -- sorry, Mr. -- no, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- I will respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You were not attacked for going into an irrelevant area at all. You were attacked for asking the general to speculate. What you think Izetbegovic wanted. If you ask him what indicia he saw or what his interpretation of something that he witnessed was, that's one thing; but if you ask him to tell us what Izetbegovic was thinking out of his conception, I think that in fact is a bit speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's given an opinion about Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm showing that Izetbegovic is not the person that he thought he is. Now -- we can see clearly through this. If the gentleman really was an honest negotiator, then he wouldn't be playing these games. And what I'm doing is impeaching, actually, in a subtle way, General Praljak's impression of Izetbegovic. He thought -- and the question came directly from President Antonetti. And nobody -- no one from the Bench or the Prosecution objected that he was asked to speculate. He was giving an opinion as to the gentleman's character. Now I'm going through here and I'm asking him, you know, does this reflect, you know, the opinion that he shared? And we can see here -- that's why we went through the various pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if my technique is off, I'll try to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm trying to assist you in that, and maybe if you asked: Do you maintain that view? How do you conciliate what you find here with what you have expressed before, I think that would be main-stream cross --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- as I have learned inter alia from you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will endeavour to improve my technique and I will begin so immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Suffice it to say, it was at this particular meeting or shortly before or after -- I believe it was before when Mr. Susak who at the time was the defence minister indicates that a gentlemen's agreement had been reached?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say just one thing before I answer your question, Mr. Karnavas, if you will give me a minute. You misunderstood my characterisation of Mr. Izetbegovic. I was talking about his civility, his courtesy in talks. I never had any doubts about Mr. Izetbegovic's policies. So please do not get the two confused. I was talking about a genteel person, gentleman, but not about my interpretation of his positions. After the meeting in Mostar, which took more than an hour and a half, I knew perfectly well and also on the basis of the Islamic Declaration, I knew what policy would be pursued with a great deal of certainty. So these are two different things. Secondly, if you allow me, regarding Ahtisaari, Mr. Izetbegovic had already signed the constitutional principles and Mr. Ahtisaari says at the time, You signed and now if you declare this null and void, the war will go on, and Mr. Izetbegovic did cancel it. And he establishes a committee. And you know what Churchill said, if you want not to solve things, set up a committee. In other words, if an agreement had been reached and signed, then you have to implement it. You don't set up arbitration commissions because arbitration commissions arbitrate over things that have not been agreed. If something has been agreed, then there's no need for an arbitration commission. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Praljak, and in fact we can see that on page 44 that's exactly what Mr. Boban tells us. Where he says: "I think that if we must look" -- this would be on -- the last three numbers would be 286 so you can find that. He says: "That's why I think that if we must look for a committee or arbiters between us here and we are here, then I think nothing will come of our cooperation. At the same time, this means that somebody does not want agreement. We are for agreement. I think arbitrators and committees should be set up between Muslims and the Serbs, the Croats and the Serbs, and not at all between the Muslims and the Croats. We meet every day, Mr. Izetbegovic, and I spend dozens of hours talking and making arrangements. It all has come to nothing." Now, this is what's being said at this point in time, yet as I understand it, it was your understanding at the time that an agreement had indeed been reached, and as a result, that's what you communicated in Mostar, which then we have the decision of January 15, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was reached and signed, Mr. Karnavas. The agreement was reached and it was signed. The -- when they came to Zagreb, the constitutional solutions were already in place and they needed to be implemented. And I took part in some talks with Mr. Izetbegovic, not this one, but the talks about the agreement on how to avoid the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could look at now -- at P 01150 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, it's almost time for the break, so maybe it's best if we look at this document after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. And, Your Honour, I am going to be referring to another document as well in a very short period of time. I wonder if I could give directions to General Praljak so he will know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have ten minutes, ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, very well. I think I can finish this chapter and then move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at P 01150 and this is January 16, 1993, and we can see this comes from Bozo Rajic, and we can see the goal that the -- what the goal is in the very preamble, "with the goal of establishing peace on the whole territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and protecting citizens and their property," and then he hereby orders it. And this is based on what you had communicated to Mr. Rajic, who at the time was the minister of defence for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Rajic received this order which had been agreed on by Mr. Izetbegovic, the co-chairman; Gojko Susak; and I worked on the implementation, and I took part in a great deal of the talks and I drafted this together with Mr. Izetbegovic. And the order that was worded in this manner was handed to Mr. Rajic to -- who was a minister in Mr. Izetbegovic's government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at 1D 01195, 1D 01195, this is from a newspaper article dated 21 January 1993, and it's an interview with Bozo Rajic, minister of defence. Okay. We cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think if you could somehow enlarge -- that's the best we can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I just want to go over some things that Mr. Rajic said. He was asked: "To what extent and in how much of the sovereign state of BH are you able to perform your duties as minister of defence?" And he says, the latter part of this paragraph: "I intend to create a Ministry of Defence appropriate to the model and needs of a sovereign state. Although incomplete, my information indicates that the current ministry is just a government office at the level of a Registry, an extension of the BH army Main Staff. There is no concept in which it can or should be that ..." Now, is he making a correct statement to your understanding? If you don't know, don't speculate. All right. Let me repeat it again. He states in here that he intends "to create a Ministry of Defence appropriate to the model and needs of a sovereign state. Although incomplete, my information indicates that the current ministry is just a government office at the level of a Registry, an extension of the BH army Main Staff. There is no concept in which it can or should be that ..." Now, to your understanding, is Mr. Rajic correct in the manner in which he's describing what the Ministry of Defence is at that point in time when he's serving as minister of defence for BiH?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was worse than Mr. Rajic describes it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And let's go to the second page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Further down in the -- he's asked: "The order stipulates that the commanders of all three armies in BH will submit regular reports to you as minister of defence and that each army will conditionally withdraw to their own provinces ..." So further down, that's the part I want to reference you to, he states: "To be honest" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is in the first paragraph, Your Honour, right after that, in the middle of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "To be honest, I did not expect that the BH army would do so emphatic -- would be so emphatic in its rejection of this plan, which is, in fact, simply the implementation of the agreement from Geneva. It is amazing that circles in the BH army do not see the particular effectiveness of an order like this. Why? Because it assumes the withdrawal of each army to its own provinces ..." Later on he says: "However, sometimes in politics a very short time is sufficient to make a serious volte face. I believe profoundly that after two rounds of negotiations in Geneva, if not before, everything will be different and on new grounds." He continues: "There are several reasons why I issued an order of this kind. I wanted there to be a true ray of peace. I believe that the Ministry of Defence must make a statement in this regard, albeit at a junction -- at a juncture when it was unacceptable to attempt to place the entire area and everything that is happening in it in the services of one interest, that being the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina such as it is and such as it can be. "Furthermore, I felt as a Croat in BH that I should say that we recognise the state of BH. I wanted to reaffirm the suspended offices of state, the Presidency, the Government, and the Ministry of Defence and to tell people that defence was returning as an active office in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Finally, I wanted to score some points on the eve of the continuation of the Geneva negotiations, to give the politicians and negotiators another argument to link the armies in BH to a single place for discussion and decision-making ..." And then he talks about his good intentions. To your understanding, is Bozo Rajic, the way he's describing the events here, is he correct? I mean, was it necessary at the time to link-up -- was it necessary for the Ministry of Defence to have some authority?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If there is a minister and the Ministry of Defence, then they were supposed to do their job, at least with regard to the armies that obeyed to them, and those were the BH army and the HVO. The Serbs, the Republika Srpska army, they of course had their own plans, the BH army had its own plans, and the only ones who were constantly open to negotiations to the setting up of a joint command, who supported all international treaties, were Croats, both the Presidency and the government, both Croatia and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark, could the witness please repeat who else was in favour of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and everybody was hoping that something would happen in the next round of talks. Let me tell you one thing. In order to resolve a situation, to find a remedy, you have to recognise the symptoms. And I'm telling you that the symptoms in Bosnia and Herzegovina show that that was cancer and all the international agents were treating flu, and here you have the misconceptions that resulted from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's finish with this document so we can take the break. I just need a couple of minutes. If we go on to the next page, page 3, because it ties in with your answer here. On the second paragraph where it says: "The latest incident in Gornji Vakuf demonstrates that these two destructive factors in the BH army notwithstanding there is political leadership in this entire operation. Recent orders from the BH army Main Staff and statements from Alija Izetbegovic have unambiguously indicated that the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, stands as the political body atop this command period -- pyramid, and that the fighting is being waged by directive in a clear mission to obstruct the Geneva process and if not possible to exclude them entirely, to develop -- to devalue the achievements particularly of the Croatian people. It is also another attempt, albeit by means of violence, to establish a civic, unitary, and centralised state. If in the past we guess that the security -- if in the past we guessed and secretly wished that this was simply a case of extremism, on this occasion we have to say this is a matter of politics of the organised and deliberate conduct of those operations. This is a battle for land to destroy the Vance-Owen project." Now, this is his obvious -- interpretation of the events, but you were there, you knew what was happening on the ground, you met with Izetbegovic. Can you please tell us whether Mr. Rajic is accurate in his accounting of what the intents are?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with Mr. Rajic's analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'll leave it at that for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can take our break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First we're going to go to a document to kind of round this area up, another Presidential transcript and then we will go to a map to discuss the issue that was brought up earlier with Judge Trechsel's question. So first let's look at P 01240, P 01240. This is a Presidential transcript. It's dated 20 January 1993, so this would have been five days after the previous transcript that we looked at, and I'm going to direct your attention to page 5 -- the discussion actually begins on page 4, it's Mr. Akmadzic, we saw him here, and there is a discussion about Gornji Vakuf and it says in the middle of the paragraph -- or for your purposes, General Praljak, it's 3 -- so it will be 301 and 302, those are the pages that you need to look at. And we see in the middle it says: "... Mr. Izetbegovic refused at the meeting today -- refused at the meeting today, although in Geneva he said he accepted that there was no dispute over the provinces that belonged to the Croatian people conditionally and the provinces that belonged to the Muslim people." So he refused to go to Geneva but he made this conditional acceptance. But then if we go to page -- further down, I believe it's 19 -- 19 in English and if you could look at 317, the last numbers on the page would be 316 to 317. Here we have Lord Owen. He says: "We know because Mr. Izetbegovic gave an official statement that he would accept the constitutional principles and the cease-fire document although Silajdzic constantly tried to drive him off that course. However, in recent weeks I still think that they have shown more willingness to be involved in the Geneva process and we may be able to keep them on this course. And this may be the right moment now to talk about the provisional government or the interim government. Mr. Vance also agreed with this." To your understanding -- we have here Lord Owen saying that Izetbegovic offered an official statement agreeing to the constitutional principles. Do you know whether Izetbegovic -- do you know whether Izetbegovic kept that agreement or kept that promise, to accept the constitutional principles? It's cause for a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at the next para -- the next portion of this document because we have the president - and this would be President Tudjman - he says: "I would add, what may influence Izetbegovic in further talks is the fact which I mentioned to the gentlemen up there, that they asked us yesterday and today to continue aircraft support for their forces in the Bihac area and to transfer two helicopters to them. I don't know whether you know, gentlemen, that a ship was confiscated in the Adriatic Sea yesterday. It carried wheat, but also some serious weapons, apparently from Pakistan. It can be assumed, if that is the case, that this was sent to them, so in their belligerence they will have to face the problem of how to continue the war if they can't secure, and the ship was stopped by the peacekeeping force in the Otranto and examined in the Adriatic port ..." And here's what I want to focus on a little bit. What is Mr. -- what is President Tudjman talking about, if you know, that is, when he says that the "continued aircraft support for the forces in the Bihac area ..." What is he talking about? Who is providing that support?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian state and the Croatian air force constantly, without any interruptions, provided support to the Bihac region, and only thanks to that the Bihac region managed to survive until the Croatian army liberated the area. I am fully aware of that as a participant and one of the organisers of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when he's talking about weapons being -- apparently coming from Pakistan being confiscated, to your knowledge was there -- was that permissible at the time, for weapons to be --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And were the helicopters being used also to transport weapons or to assist the Muslim forces in transporting weapons from Croatia to the Bihac area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At the time was there an embargo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I may be -- this may call for speculation, but do you think that Mr. Vance, who was for the United Nations, and Mr. Owen, who was for the European Union, would have heard that there had been an embargo? Or was that something secret that nobody would have known about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were aware of the embargo. It was no secret. This was done pursuant to a decision by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, in your meetings, at least when you were present, do you recall at any time these negotiators, Vance or Owen, or anyone else advocating that Croatia not provide assistance to the Muslim forces in BiH, not provide military assistance, transport weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They knew -- the Americans and everybody else were aware of the assistance being provided, regardless of the embargo, and so on and so forth. Everyone turned a blind eye, and as time went on, that practice became more frequent. Weapons came from Turkey, Iran, and so on and so forth. The first flight from Iran, the Americans requested for the weapons to be seized. They knew what flight the arms were on, what kind of arms. Their information was complete. Some of the weapons were destroyed, and to the rest they just turned a blind eye and allowed the weapons to stay on the flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karnavas, in the transcript here -- I'm aware of the transcript and there are two very important things, the first being that in Sarajevo Izetbegovic did not want two members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croats, to participate in the conversations, he wanted to eliminate them; and secondly, after the defeat of his aggression in Vakuf he accused Croatia of holding tank brigades over there and he wanted that problem to be raised before the Security Council of the United Nations. When that fell through, when that occupation fell through in Gornji Vakuf after a large number of our casualties, he accused Croatia that it had sent a number of brigades over there which is a notorious lie and a sheer impertinence. Akmadzic says it very expressly that this is a lie, that this is not true. However, many did not accept that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just deal with that very quickly. I didn't want to spend too much time with document, but first of all, who are the two members of the Presidency that Izetbegovic did not want them attending, that you make reference to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boras and Lasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the next part was with respect to Gornji Vakuf you said that Izetbegovic wanted to go before the United Nations and, as I understand it, accuse the Republic of Croatia as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and President Tudjman says here before Owen, he presents a problem to Owen and says, What do I say to the international community when they hear such blatant lies? And Mr. Owen says to him, Try to pursue your principal policy, try to calm things down because they knew that that was not true. I can refer you to a number of pages where you can find that if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will be able to see that, but I guess just touching on that point because on the one hand, you got weapons going in with the assistance, to a great extent, of United Nations countries, including members of the Security Council. They either know or they're assisting in the process. And on the other hand, you have -- and that's for the benefit of Izetbegovic. And now Izetbegovic at the same time wants to turn around and complain to the very same institution that somehow the Croats are responsible for Gornji Vakuf. That's what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall at any point in time Izetbegovic -- I mean, President Tudjman ever saying that the time has come where we simply have to stop assisting the Muslims? Cut the -- stop them at the border, don't let any of their refugees come in. The ones that are in country, send them back or send them to some neighbour countries like Slovenia or Hungary, stop providing the aid. Did you ever hear President Tudjman say that, given the way Izetbegovic and his cohorts were behaving and acting towards the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever said that, Tudjman, the government, Gojko Susak, myself, nobody. Truth be told, Izetbegovic actually believed that Croatia should be his springboard for the fight against Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we just yielded into that. Croatia served as the logistical, organisational and every other base for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for their attacks against the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's how things went on throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we go to the next document perhaps we can look at the map and kind of just deal with that matter. 1D 02843 -- it's in e-court -- it will be in e-court. And then maybe you could point out the two areas that I had mentioned earlier. And -- now, I know that there's -- you've covered -- you have a code and it covers -- you'll see the code covers the municipalities, the entire portions of the municipalities. But I first want you to just look at that and orientate yourself and then if you could find, for instance, the Teslic area, it says --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you have Usora.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1, if you will, Usora. Here's Teslic, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you put like 1 for Usora and 2 for Teslic, just so we have it later on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did -- the HVO existed in all those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the big map that I drew which I used to show where the HVO was, I forgot to say that there was also one in Olovo. There was a small HVO unit in Olovo. I would like to add that to the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you look at this particular map - and as I indicated, it's coloured where -- we've coloured the entire municipalities - can you tell us with any degree of certainty whether the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna covered that entire area or whether it covered portions of various municipalities as depicted in this colour-coded map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It covered parts of the municipalities where the Croatian population was compact in one way or another, maybe in three villages or five or in small part of the municipality. For example, like in Olovo they were not numerous but they managed to organise themselves and put together a unit comprising several hundred people that were willing to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If any of the member of the Bench has any questions on this, otherwise I will be asking for an IC number and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give an IC number, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This document shall be given Exhibit IC 01032.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Seeing no questions from the Bench I'll move on to the next document, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While we still have this on, we've heard there were HVO in these communes. That is not to say that they are regarded as belonging to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was later on that they assembled into Herceg-Bosna, but it was not a well-rounded territory that could be separated from the rest. It's impossible. In Olovo there were four [as interpreted] villages that were Herceg-Bosna in a part that had a majority Muslim population and we fought in that area together. We're talking about defence operations in the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm quite aware of how complicated matters were ethnically, but on the list of municipalities forming the HZ HB they do not figure, do they, in the list of 18 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Usora is on the list. It has made it to the list, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, you can see there is a colour code and there is exhibit numbers or document numbers. This map was made based on these exhibits which are already in the evidence, which -- and that forms the basis for this colour-coded map. So in the event you wish further clarification, we can go to the documents, I can do that tomorrow if necessary. Well, I'm hoping I don't have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- but if necessary we can do that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to another document now, and we may have to spend a little bit of time on this. I'm going to fast-forward in time. We're going to look at 1D 03141 and I'm fast-forwarding in time because then we're going to -- I'm going to use this as a -- sort of a basis to go backwards. If you could give this a quick glance, first of all, and this is an article published 19 April 2002 regarding global terrorism, and it refers to a particular case, the Pogorelica case. And let me first ask you, have you heard of this particular case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look -- if we see this document it tells us that this case is about certain intelligence services, foreign intelligence services, working in conjunction with Bosniak intelligence services in BiH during and after the Dayton peace -- prior to and after the Dayton Peace Accord. Now, let me ask you this: Were you aware that the Iranian services were operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Pasdaran and another secret service, VEVAK -- I'm not sure of the exact name, it consists of four or five letters. In any case there were hundreds of them in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the whole problem, Mr. Karnavas, grew out of proportion when the Americans felt the threat coming from that group of people and when they realised that that problem had to do with the attack on some American military targets and the attack of – in New York. That's when they actually saw clearly what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But if we look through this document, at least there are claims being made that the Americans were well aware that the Iranian services - and we can see some of their handiwork today on television - that the Americans were well aware that these services were operating in Bosnia in 1993/1994 and thereafter at least. So do you know anything about that? For instance, if we were to look at page 2 where it says Bosnia and Iran, at the very last paragraph it says: "Explaining the relations with Iranian structures, Alispahic compared them for investigators as well to the level of contacts with other services and structures of Western European countries, only emphasizing" the differences ... And then he says later on that he paid an official visit to the United States in 1993, "asking their services to help us ..." In other words, to help the Bosniaks. Now I just have one question. If Alija Izetbegovic is the president of the Presidency and if he is supposedly representing the entire nation, how is it - assuming this is correct - he's trying to engage foreign services to operate in Bosnia on behalf of only his people or his party?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Alija Izetbegovic never gave up on the foundations that he presented in his Islamic Declaration. Mr. Karnavas, what the American other secret services knew was not accepted by their respective politicians until the incident in New York when the two towers collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to page 3, at the very top it says: "The sources familiar with the intelligence situation in Sarajevo during the war" -- this would be page 1D 51-1814. It says: "The sources familiar with the intelligence situation in Sarajevo during the war explain that MUP and AID, AID, held at the same time relations with Iranians, American, French, and Italian intelligence services. At a time, Dani published a statement of H.K. Roy, head of CIA, in Sarajevo, stating that in the summer of 1995 Nedzad Ugljen" - and I'm mispronouncing the name - "had betrayed him to the head of the Iranian intelligence services in Sarajevo ..." We don't have to go on. But MUP we're talking about the Ministry of the Interior, AID, that's the Muslim services; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Maybe I can say something else, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Roy saved his head by fleeing Sarajevo after he heard that the Iranians were getting ready to assassinate him. He had helpers, and I'm not going to go into that, but all I want to say is that he saved himself by fleeing Sarajevo but just barely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, there are rumours that the Izetbegovic -- I don't want to say "government," but Izetbegovic or his -- and/or his followers were also engaged in sort of assassinations, political assassinations, as you know, one being against Mr. Halilovic after Mr. Halilovic had a fall-out with SDA?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection to questions about rumours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's not a rumour that his wife and his brother-in-law were killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to counsel giving evidence, Mr. President. If he wants to ask the witness if he has knowledge about such things, but again, rumours and counsel just giving his own evidence or suggestions to the witness in advance of questions is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please put a question to the witness and the witness will provide you with what you're expecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the bottom -- further down we can see that there was an agreement that was signed with the Americans, with General Wesley Clark, on 12 February 1996, and then four days later, the very last paragraph, we see that there was an air-drop in the Pogorelica, this camp. And we can see here -- and there's a quotation by Bradley Graham "about 200 Iranian military instructors were still in Bosnia," and Mr. Graham -- and this is on 1D 51-1815, that's the page number. He says: "'Their base camp is in Fojnica, some 30 miles north-west from Sarajevo. There is concern that Iranians and Bosnians are now trying to find a new status for their guard members by turning them into civilian trainers, instead of military instructors,' said the US officer monitoring in the region." And then if we turn the next page, we see here at the very -- at the second paragraph: "By use of helicopter and transporters, IF OR forces occupied the camp and arrested, in the building or in -- or on the way there eight Bosnians and three Iranians. US Admiral Leighton Smith visited the camp the day after and unusually severely condemned the activities there: "'One does not have to be a genius to realise that what we found here was obviously a terrorist training course ... nor can one deny that the terrorist training in this camp was being carried out in direct cooperation with the people from the government ...'" IFOR is the international force at the time; correct, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And through a classical military operation those forces stormed the camp, arrested and found all the documents that made them conclude that this was a terrorist training camp. Of course they belonged to al-Qaeda as it turned out later; that's number one. Second of all, this person --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may I get in the record an objection based on the time-frame of this issue which is from February of 1996. So we object as irrelevant and beyond the time-frame of the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would appreciate if the gentleman would wait for the answer first; and second of all, Mr. Stringer wasn't here at the time when they brought in testimony and we wasted approximately two weeks of time with a Mr. Miller regarding the so-called joint criminal enterprise extending well beyond. At the time I objected loud and vociferously. The Trial Chamber decided nonetheless to hear the evidence. And so when we're -- I'm moving backwards. What I'm trying to show is that even after Dayton and signing all these agreements to behave, there is Izetbegovic pursuing his goal, a goal that started way before which is why Izetbegovic never wanted to put forward his proposal as to how Bosnia-Herzegovina should be governed internally. Therefore, there was no joint criminal enterprise on the part of the Croats, but rather on the part of the Muslims headed by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just two quick responses, Mr. President. I was here when Mr. Miller testified. Again, we object to the speeches by counsel. It's more speech than cross-examination and questions to the General. So our objection is still that it's beyond the scope of the indictment in that it relates to February 1996 which is well beyond the time-frame of the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you're saying that the joint criminal enterprise started before 1992 and continued after 1995, then there should be no problem; but what the Defence is trying to tell us through its questions is that Mr. Izetbegovic continued with its own enterprise which was to Islamize the country after 1996 and I guess he wants to make a parallel between the two -- at least that's what I think. Mr. Karnavas, am I right or wrong or did I understand what you were trying to demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct, Mr. President. This is -- and I want to make sure because there is always this argument about a tu quoque. This has nothing to do with tu quoque. This has to do exactly with the MO of Alija Izetbegovic, and it is our contention that one party would move earnestly and they were led to believe that they could move earnestly in a particular direction, only to later find out that there was no agreement and then complaints were being made to the Security Council. And so that's our -- that is our position because the main interlocutor for the Muslims is Alija Izetbegovic. And he'd been portrayed as the president of a country with the ABiH as the army for the country when in fact he's there for one constituent nation. And we grant him his right to fight for that particular nation, but he's certainly not there as an honest broker trying to assist everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's our main position and I think it's assistant with attacking the Prosecution's theory of the case, which is joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, it's a quarter to 2.00. Time flies with you. I'm sure we'll come back to this document tomorrow morning, so we'll keep it close at hand. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. I wish you all a good afternoon.
